title: Rivian Expands Redwood Battery Partnership
content:
Rivian and Redwood Materials expanded their battery partnership on October 14 to cover manufacturing scrap, retired electric-vehicle packs and stationary storage. The companies’ announcement outlines a route for batteries to keep working after vehicle service before their materials are recovered.

Rivian’s service centers will collect packs that are no longer suitable for vehicles. Redwood will assess whether each pack can serve in an energy-storage installation or should go to recycling. The expanded agreement also includes battery scrap from Rivian’s manufacturing operations.

The arrangement builds on a 10 megawatt-hour storage project announced in April for Rivian’s factory in Normal, Illinois. That is an energy-capacity figure, not a 10 MW power rating. The announcement does not establish how long the system could support the factory’s full load.

In its October 14 social post, Redwood frames electricity availability and the wait for grid infrastructure as central industrial constraints. Its approach combines recovered packs with power electronics and control software, allowing batteries with different histories to operate within one managed storage system.

For a factory, storage can charge when conditions are favorable and discharge during expensive peaks. That can reduce electricity demand charges, depending on the tariff and operating schedule. It is an application of behind-the-meter energy storage: shifting when a site draws power rather than creating electricity.

Inc.’s October 14 reporting says the Illinois project remains in design, planning and permitting, with operation targeted as early as the third quarter of 2027. The 10 MWh installation should therefore be treated as planned capacity, with timing subject to project execution.

When reuse is no longer practical, Redwood says its recycling process can recover more than 95% of selected critical minerals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper. That is a company-reported recovery figure; it does not mean every pack retains 95% of its original energy capacity.

The wider question is whether repurposing can deliver dependable storage at a competitive installed cost. As with the broader battery-storage economics debate, pack availability alone does not settle the cost of integration, maintenance or delivered electricity. This announcement supplies a lifecycle plan, not independently verified operating results.
